title: Spanish Omelette (Tortilla)
subtitle: thick potato and egg tortilla, warm or at room temperature
excerpt: A Spanish tortilla is thick, golden, and sliceable -- nothing like a French omelette. Potato and onion are cooked slowly in olive oil first, then bound together with egg. It is just as good at room temperature as warm, making it a perfect lunch or tapas dish.
sourceNotes: Tortilla española is one of the most widely eaten dishes in Spain. Its origins are debated but it became the national dish of everyday cooking by the 19th century. The version with onion is common in the south; without is more typical in the north.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 4 hours ahead. Serve at room temperature.

content.text: The flip is the hardest part. Slide the tortilla onto a large plate, then invert the pan over the plate and flip both together so the tortilla lands back uncooked-side down.

Heat the oil in a 24cm frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the potato and onion. Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring often, until the potato is tender but not coloured. Drain through a colander, reserving the oil.
Beat the eggs with salt in a bowl. Add the potato and onion. Mix gently. Leave for 5 minutes.
Heat 2 tablespoons of the reserved oil in the pan over medium heat. Pour in the egg and potato mixture. Spread evenly. Cook for 5 minutes until the base is set.
Slide the tortilla onto a large plate. Place the pan over it and flip so the tortilla is uncooked side down. Cook for another 4 to 5 minutes.
Slide onto a plate. Rest for 5 minutes before slicing. Serve warm or at room temperature.

items.symptom: Tortilla stuck to the pan when flipping
items.cause: Not enough oil in the pan or undercooked base
items.fix: Make sure the base is fully set before flipping and use enough oil.

items.symptom: Centre is raw after the flip
items.cause: Heat too high, outer cooked before the inside set
items.fix: Keep the heat medium-low and give it longer.

content.text: Tortilla española is the kind of dish that every Spanish cook has their own version of. It is served in tapas bars, packed for picnics, eaten cold from the fridge at midnight. The two-ingredient version -- potato and egg only -- has its defenders, but most home cooks add onion. Either way, it is one of the great simple dishes of European cooking.
